confidence_note: The old Alexander the Great story is not in the book and was replaced by the book's own opening case, Kennedy in the Cuban Missile Crisis, checked against the archive.org full text. Holiday's interpretive claims (Kennedy 'saved the world') are kept as the author's view; secondary details like the Turkey missile deal are as Holiday tells them.
facts: Between going to bed on October 15, 1962 and waking the next morning, the CIA identified Soviet ballistic missile sites being built in Cuba, ninety miles from US shores.
As many as seventy million people were expected to die in the first exchange of strikes, though Holiday notes that was only a guess.
Kennedy's record was poor: the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in April 1961, which the CIA pressured him into, and being dominated by Khrushchev in Vienna.
His advisors were immediate and emphatic: destroy the sites with full military force, then a full-scale invasion of Cuba.
He had recently read Barbara Tuchman's The Guns of August, about leaders rushing into World War I and being unable to stop; he wanted everyone to slow down.

In his notes he repeated words: 'Missile. Missile. Missile.', 'Veto. Veto. Veto. Veto.'; on a yellow legal pad he drew two sailboats; on White House stationery he wrote: 'We are demanding withdrawal of the missiles.'
He asked advisors why the Russians had done this and what advantage they wanted.
He chose a blockade, opposed by nearly half his advisors, because it preserved options and used time as a tool; he called it a 'quarantine'.

After the quarantine came provocations: a Russian tanker approached the quarantine line, Soviet submarines surfaced, and an American U-2 spy plane was shot down over Cuba, killing the pilot. Kennedy told advisors his worry was not the first step but both sides escalating to the fourth and fifth.
In tense moments he walked in the Rose Garden, swam, sat in his rocking chair, and left the room so advisors could debate freely.

On October 26, eleven days in, Khrushchev wrote that they were pulling on a rope with a knot of war in the middle; the Soviets signalled they would remove the missiles. Kennedy pledged not to invade Cuba.
In secret, Kennedy also let the Russians know he would remove US missiles in Turkey, months later, so as not to appear pressured.
scene_details: two sailboats drawn on a yellow legal pad
'Missile. Missile. Missile.' repeated in his notes
Khrushchev's rope with a knot of war in the middle
tension: Every advisor says strike now; the last time Kennedy followed that kind of pressure he got the Bay of Pigs.
opening_idea: Open on the night of October 15, 1962: Kennedy goes to bed, and while he sleeps the CIA finds the missile sites.

lessons.idea: Before a big decision, buy time and widen the options instead of taking the first forceful one.
lessons.anchor: The blockade kept options open and gave Khrushchev time.
lessons.example: A manager furious about a client email drafts a reply, then asks a colleague what the client might want before sending.

reflect_final: In a decision you are facing now, which option would keep the most doors open for a few more days?

use_cases.situation: A meeting is rushing toward a drastic decision.
use_cases.move: Ask what the other side is trying to get, the question Kennedy put to his advisors, before voting.

use_cases.situation: You are about to send an angry reply to a relative.
use_cases.move: Write what you actually want from them in one sentence, like Kennedy's note, then decide.
Choose the step that can still be reversed and set a date to look again.

pocket_idea: Kennedy wrote one sentence of what he wanted before choosing; write yours before you act.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: In the tensest days of the missile crisis Kennedy doodled two sailboats on a legal pad.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Missiles found in Cuba; advisors demand strike and invasion; Kennedy, burned by the Bay of Pigs and fresh from The Guns of August, slows everyone down, asks why the Soviets did it, picks a 'quarantine'; Khrushchev writes about the knot and pulls back.
conversation_variants.question_idea: When did slowing down save you from a mistake?
